new_statements.quote: p. 85-86: "In terms of suprasegmental features, ’Olekha also has tone, vowel length, nasalization, and glottalization. [...] Tonal minimal pairs show contrastive tone following sonorant initials, a system which is reminiscent of East Bodish languages [...] We also heard stress without glottalization, in which case it is characterized by a slight increase in intensity, pitch, and vowel length." p. 90: "Note, importantly, that the stress pattern in this word is different than the stress pattern of the other kinship terms. While all the other forms in Table 5 have word-initial stress, ‘grandmother’ has word-final stress. Given that word-initial stress is also a feature of Dzongkha and the East Bodish languages, it seems plausible the kinship terms [...] were borrowed from Dzongkha, while the word for ‘grandmother,’ representing an original stress pattern, is an older term in the language."

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog lists the language with an empty rule and no existing statements; Hyslop 2016 supplies the first statement: contrastive tone plus a word-stress description (initial in probable Dzongkha loans, non-initial/final in older indigenous vocabulary). It does not contradict anything because the catalog records nothing to contradict.
new_statements.rule_in_words: ’Olekha has contrastive tone (clearest after sonorant initials, East Bodish-style; also e.g. tɔ ‘cooked rice’ vs tɔ́ ‘horse’) and also word stress, realised as a slight rise in intensity, pitch and vowel length, sometimes co-occurring with glottalization. Stress placement is not given as a single rule: most kinship terms (likely Dzongkha loans) carry word-initial stress, ‘grandmother’ ʔɐˈpeŋ carries word-final stress, and the author notes (p. 96) 'a tendency for more indigenous words to have glottal stops and non-initial stress'. Transcribed forms show both initial (ˈhoʔma, ˈkɣgɣ, ˈpandala, ˈkaʃalo) and non-initial (ɑˈnɔk, iŋˈnɔk, hoˈʔoŋ, guˈluŋ, ɐˈmik, ʔɐˈpʰɪt, sɔʁoʔˈla) stress, so placement looks lexical/stratum-dependent rather than fixed. Fn. 8 (p. 87): tone marked only where certain, stress marked where clear; 'it was not obvious that tone and stress were necessarily features of every word'; both are probably underreported.
new_statements.exceptions: ‘grandmother’ ʔɐˈpeŋ has word-final stress against the initial stress of the other kinship terms (p. 90); indigenous (non-borrowed) words tend toward non-initial stress and glottal stops, though 'these features are not found exclusively in non-native words' (p. 96). Author cautions the analysis is preliminary (one elderly fluent speaker plus two semi-speakers) and that tone and stress may not be features of every word.
new_statements.identity_note: Hyslop 2016 describes ’Olekha, 'the variety of Black Mountain Mönpa spoken in Rukha village of south central Wangdi' (p. 80), from one fluent native speaker in her 80s and two semi-speakers (data collected 2010 and 2012). Black Mountain Mönpa is spoken in at least six villages; the Rukha variety is the one documented here, so the stress remarks are specific to Rukha ’Olekha.

audit.reasoning: Quote check: every clause of the deciding quotation and the secondary 2016 passages was found verbatim in the held PDFs at the stated locators (Hyslop 2023 p.111 paras 4-5 and exx. 5-8; Hyslop 2016 p.86 sec.3.1, sec.4 kinship paragraph, sec.5, fn.8). The classification (lexical stress, initial or final, no weight/positional rule) matches what the sources say and what the 18 stress-marked forms in Hyslop 2016 show.
